bridge: I03 introduced tenant-safe retrieval. Use fictional records and a diagram of stores and external services.
teaching:
### Ask whether the data is needed

Identify the purpose of each field before sending it to a model. Remove unnecessary identifiers and private content. Replacing a name with a code may reduce exposure but does not guarantee anonymity when other details identify the person.

### Follow every copy

A prompt may pass through an application log, provider service, debugging tool and chat-history store. Record which copies exist, who can access them and how long they remain. Check actual provider and account settings for any real use; do not infer a retention promise from a product label.

### Keep account boundaries intact

Permissions apply to retrieved text, summaries, exports and caches too. A summary of private data can remain private even if it is shorter than the source.

### Check output disclosure

The model may repeat sensitive input or unsupported personal claims. Limit access before generation and handle output appropriately. A request to “forget” a secret in later text does not erase copies already stored elsewhere.

### Plan removal and incidents

Define deletion, correction and access procedures under the applicable service and legal rules. In the fictional exercise, mark which party controls each copy so a removal request has a real owner rather than an uncheckable promise.
example:
Synthetic record
user=A; email=learner@example.invalid; note="review chapter 3";
secret_marker=DEMO-DO-NOT-SEND
Task: suggest a study schedule from chapter completion.
Needed: completed chapter IDs and available study time.
Unneeded: email, secret_marker, private free-text notes.
Safe fixture payload: {"completed":[1,2],"minutes":30}
explanation: The strongest reduction here is not sending unnecessary fields in the first place. A redactor that misses a secret marker then has less work to fail at. A real data-flow record must also include who receives the permitted payload and how long it is retained.
exercise: Create a source-to-destination inventory for the supplied task. Include application storage, model provider, logs and user display. Decide permitted fields and retention purpose for each. Identify two derived artifacts needing the same privacy review.
solution: For this fictional schedule task, application storage holds owner-scoped completed chapter IDs and available minutes; email, secret_marker and free-text note contents are excluded from the schedule payload. If a provider is used, its permitted payload is only {"completed":[1,2],"minutes":30}, under a verified service/account retention policy. Logs should record a safe task/result identifier and necessary status rather than the omitted fields. Display the schedule only to the authorised learner and retain/export/delete it under the chosen product policy. Review cached schedules and embeddings/summaries too: derived format alone does not make them anonymous. Do not invent a universal retention period or send this fixture to a provider for the exercise.
challenge: A provider setting excludes prompts from training but retains operational logs temporarily. Explain why “not trained on” and “not stored” are different claims, and propose what documentation a deployment owner must verify.
challenge_solution: Confirm retention, access, region, subprocessors and deletion terms for the actual service/account configuration. Training exclusion does not imply zero retention. Keep any personal-data legal conclusion tied to the relevant authority and contract.
